intro: Boston lost its two most famous trees long ago: the Liberty Tree to a Loyalist axe in 1775 and the Great Elm of the Common to a storm in 1876. What survived is stranger. Two English elms have flanked the Shaw Memorial since around 1800, and the Arnold Arboretum keeps accession cards on its trees like a library catalogue. The ten below split into a Common and Public Garden pair, an Arboretum six including a bonsai begun in 1737, and two across the river in Cambridge; all are free.
meta_description: Boston's remarkable trees, from the elms flanking the Shaw Memorial to a tree extinct in the wild at the Arnold Arboretum. Locations, stories, sources.
question_meta: Boston's oldest documented trees are the Shaw Memorial elms on the Common, planted between 1772 and 1812. Their story, and nine more remarkable trees.
question_answer: The oldest documented landscape trees in Boston are the two English Elms flanking the Shaw Memorial on Boston Common, planted between 1772 and 1812. The oldest living thing on this list is older still and fits on a table: the Larz Anderson Hinoki Cypress at the Arnold Arboretum, a bonsai begun in 1737.
question_context: Boston's relationship with its trees is a long ledger of documented losses, and that is precisely what makes the survivors verifiable. The Liberty Tree, the elm under which the Sons of Liberty gathered, was felled by Loyalists in August 1775 and the city has marked the spot ever since. The Great Elm of the Common, once called the city's oldest inhabitant, blew down in 1876 and was mourned in print. The Public Garden's lagoon willow, the most photographed tree in the city, collapsed as recently as July 2026. Each loss was recorded, which means each survivor stands in an unusually well-documented landscape. The Shaw Memorial elms have flanked their spot through all of it, planted in the decades around 1800 when the Common's tree-lined malls were laid out. Across town the Arnold Arboretum, founded 1872 and run by Harvard, keeps accession cards on its collection the way a library catalogues books, which is how a white oak that predates the Arboretum and a Franklinia extinct in the wild both carry paperwork most ancient trees never get.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Boston?
faq.a: The two English Elms flanking the Shaw Memorial on Boston Common, planted between 1772 and 1812, are the oldest documented trees growing in Boston ground. The oldest living thing on the list is the Larz Anderson Hinoki Cypress at the Arnold Arboretum, a bonsai begun in Japan in 1737.

faq.q: Is the Liberty Tree still standing?
faq.a: No. The Liberty Tree, the elm where Boston's revolutionary protests gathered, was felled by Loyalists in August 1775. A plaque and a bas-relief mark the site at Washington and Essex Streets; no tree on this list claims its mantle.

faq.q: Are Boston's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: All ten are free. Two stand on Boston Common and in the Public Garden, six in the Arnold Arboretum (open free daily, Orange Line to Forest Hills), and two across the river in Cambridge, at the Longfellow House and on Brattle Street.

faq.q: What is a Franklinia and why does Boston have one?
faq.a: Franklinia alatamaha is a small flowering tree that has been extinct in the wild since the early 1800s; every living one descends from seeds collected in Georgia before then. The Arnold Arboretum's specimen, accessioned in 1905, flowers in late summer.

trees.name: The Shaw Memorial Elms
trees.age_estimate: planted between 1772 and 1812, so roughly 214 to 254 years old

location.address: Boston Common, opposite 24 Beacon Street (flanking the Robert Gould Shaw Memorial, corner of Beacon and Park Streets)

trees.story: Augustus Saint-Gaudens's memorial to Robert Gould Shaw and the Massachusetts 54th was built around these two elms, not the other way round. The trees came first, planted somewhere between 1772 and 1812, probably under the 1780 permission to plant elms across from John Hancock's mansion while he was governor. The bronze arrived in 1897 and sits on a vault designed to spare their roots. The Boston Globe calls them the oldest English elms in the Western Hemisphere. One caveat on the species. Two institutional sources and the memorial's own conservation record call them English elm; a single minority account describes them as American elm. The weight of evidence sits with English elm, but the disagreement is real. Their survival is not luck. In 1927 they were written off as close to dead. The arborist Henry Davis began treating them free of charge in the 1970s and the care has never stopped: bricks packed inside the hollow trunks for stability, six to eight feet taken off the crowns in 2013, inspections every fortnight. That retrenchment pruning is what gives them the blunt, cut back outline they carry through winter. Even the cramped root vault helps, densifying the wood against Dutch elm disease. Prunings have been turned into pens and sold. The two of them stand where the Freedom Trail meets Beacon and Park, shading the regiment they now outlive by more than a century.
trees.access: Free, public park (Boston Common), directly on the Freedom Trail
trees.transport: Park Street MBTA station (Red/Green Line), roughly 3-5 minute walk

trees.name: The Peters Hill White Oak
trees.age_estimate: roughly 195 to 220 years, core-sampled in 2018 to a germination date in the early 1800s

location.address: Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University, northeast slope of Peters Hill, above the crabapple (Malus) collection
location.neighbourhood: Peters Hill, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain

trees.story: Harvard's Arnold Arboretum has been cataloguing plants since 1872 and did not get round to this one until 2010. It shows up on an 1894 city survey of Peters Hill, already growing wild on ground the Arboretum later absorbed, so when it was finally accessioned it went into the books as found growing in place rather than planted. It may be the oldest tree in the entire landscape. In 2018 a core taken from the southwest stem gave 142 countable rings, with perhaps 60 more lost in a hollow centre, putting germination in the early 1800s. It is double leadered, two stems fused near the base with the seam still visible, roughly 17 metres tall and spreading 28 metres over the crabapple collection below it. A 1927 bird's eye map of the Arboretum drew it as a lone shepherd guarding an endless flock, the flock at the time being hawthorns that have since been replaced. Two honest notes. Everything known about this tree comes from the Arboretum itself, rigorous work with published ring counts, but we found nothing independent of the institution. And no coordinates are published, so the pin is the northeast slope of Peters Hill above the crabapples rather than the trunk. Walk up the slope and look for the widest crown on the hill. At that spread it is not a difficult hunt.
verified_sources: https://arboretum.harvard.edu/arnoldia-stories/existing-through-change-quercus-alba/ (Dosmann, Michael S. 2018. 'Existing through change: Quercus alba.' Arnoldia, 76(1): 44-45.)
https://arboretum.harvard.edu/events/2025-11-15/ (Arnold Arboretum 'Tree Mob' event page, describing it as possibly the oldest accessioned tree in the landscape)
trees.access: Free, public arboretum, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Forest Hills MBTA station (Orange Line) roughly 15-20 minute walk, or bus to the Arborway/Peters Hill Gate entrance

trees.name: The Franklin Tree of the Explorers Garden
trees.age_estimate: roughly 121 years (accessioned as a rooted cutting in 1905)

location.address: Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University, Explorers Garden, Bussey Hill
location.neighbourhood: Bussey Hill, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain

trees.story: There is no wild Franklinia anywhere on earth and there has not been for about two hundred years. John Bartram found the species growing on a few acres beside the Altamaha River in Georgia in 1765, his son William collected seed around 1776, and within roughly fifty years the wild population was gone and never seen again. Every Franklin tree alive today, in every garden in the world, descends from that one collection. This is one of the oldest of them. The Arnold Arboretum took it in as a rooted cutting in 1905 from a Pennsylvania nursery, on a line traceable back to material from 1884. The International Dendrology Society, which has no stake in Harvard's reputation, calls it the largest and oldest known example of the species anywhere, and photographed it standing in October 2025. It is a small tree in the tea family and the only member of its genus, and it flowers on an odd schedule. Large cream white flowers with a boss of yellow stamens open late in the season, so the last of them are still out while the leaves around them are turning red. Seeing both at once on the same branch is the reason to come. It grows in the Explorers Garden on Bussey Hill. No coordinates are published for the individual plant, so the pin is the garden and the labels there take you the rest of the way.

best_time.label: September, when the cream flowers open while the leaves are already turning red

verified_sources: https://www.treesandshrubsonline.org/articles/franklinia/franklinia-alatamaha/ (International Dendrology Society reference site, independent of Harvard; photo dated 2025-10-27 calling it 'the largest and oldest known example of Franklinia alatamaha anywhere in the world', confirming it standing and photographed recently)
trees.access: Free, public arboretum, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Forest Hills MBTA station (Orange Line) roughly 15-20 minute walk, or bus to the Arborway entrance near Bussey Hill

trees.name: The Dawn Redwood of the Public Garden

location.address: Boston Public Garden, near the Charles Street / Beacon Street corner of the Lagoon

trees.story: Until 1944 this species was known only from fossils and assumed to have been extinct for millions of years. Then living Metasequoia turned up in Sichuan, and in early 1948 the first seeds to leave China arrived at Harvard's Arnold Arboretum in Jamaica Plain, a few miles from where this tree stands, just ahead of the door closing on scientific exchange with China for decades. The Arboretum raised seedlings and sent them around the world. This one was planted in the Public Garden in 1963, one of four here. It is not old, and it is not pretending to be. At about 63 it earns its place on what it is rather than how long it has stood. Dawn redwood is a deciduous conifer, which most people meet for the first time in autumn, when a tree that plainly looks like a redwood turns foxy orange and drops every needle it has. The trunk is fluted and deeply hollowed under each branch, another oddity of the species, and a younger 'Gold Rush' cultivar stands across the path for comparison. One note on sourcing: the 1963 planting date and the exact placement come from the Friends of the Public Garden, whose own people care for the tree, and we found no record of this specimen independent of them.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the needles turn foxy orange and fall

trees.access: Free, public park, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Arlington MBTA station (Green Line), roughly 2-3 minute walk

trees.name: The Original Dawn Redwood of the Arboretum
trees.age_estimate: roughly 77 years, grown from seed collected in Hubei, China in 1948

location.address: Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University, near the Hunnewell Visitor Center, opposite the Arborway Gate

trees.story:
This tree grew from the seed shipment that put a fossil back into the ground. In 1948 the Arnold Arboretum took delivery of seed collected in Hubei, China, from a species that had been known to science only from fossils until living trees turned up in the interior a few years earlier. The seed was raised here, and the Arboretum's own account of what came up is worth quoting: the first of its kind to grow in North America in over two million years. The accession number is 524-48. From that lot and its siblings, dawn redwoods went out to gardens across the world, which is how a tree that was a rumour inside living memory became an ordinary sight on ordinary streets.

It stands near the Hunnewell Visitor Center, opposite the Arborway Gate, so it is the first thing worth walking to once you are through. It is also fifteen years older than the dawn redwood in the Public Garden across town, and its senior in the plainest sense: same species, same 1948 seed, one generation up.

One honest note on the record. A separately numbered 1948 accession is described elsewhere as the Arboretum's oldest dawn redwood, out along Conifer Path, and we could not establish whether that is this tree under a second label or a sibling raised from the same seed. Both came off the same shipment.

best_time.label: late October into November, when a conifer this size turns rust orange and drops every needle it has

trees.access: Free, public arboretum, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Forest Hills MBTA station (Orange Line), roughly 20 minute walk to the Arborway Gate and Hunnewell Visitor Center, or the 39 bus to the Arborway stop

trees.name: The Wilson Paperbark Maple
trees.age_estimate: roughly 119 years (collected as a wild seedling in 1907)

location.address: Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University, Maple Collection, off Meadow Road
location.neighbourhood: Meadow Road, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain

trees.story:
Almost every paperbark maple in America descends from two seedlings one man dug out of a Chinese wood in the autumn of 1907. The plant collector Ernest Henry Wilson found them in forest north of Yichang, in Hubei, lifted them and shipped them to the Arnold Arboretum. Both survived. This is one of the two, accession 12488, and by the Arboretum's record the pair are the first and the oldest paperbark maples on the continent and the genetic source of most of the ones planted in the country since.

The species has gone the other way at home. Acer griseum is now endangered in the wild in China, its remaining stands small and scattered, which makes a specimen tree in Jamaica Plain a piece of conservation as much as a piece of horticulture.

Come in winter. The bark is what the tree is named for and it is the reason to make the walk: it lifts off the trunk in thin cinnamon and copper curls that stay attached rather than falling, and with the leaves gone and low sun on it the trunk is the whole show.

One note on the record. All of the above traces back to the Arboretum, including a published feature written out of its own history, so this is one institution's account, thorough and public, but not independently corroborated. No coordinates exist for the individual tree. The pin is the maple collection off Meadow Road, about ten minutes up from the Forest Hills gate.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and low winter sun catches the peeling cinnamon bark

trees.access: Free, public arboretum, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Forest Hills MBTA station (Orange Line), roughly 10-12 minute walk via the Forest Hills Gate and Meadow Road

trees.name: The Larz Anderson Hinoki Cypress

location.address: Bonsai and Penjing Pavilion, Dana Greenhouses, Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University, 1050 Centre Street
location.neighbourhood: Dana Greenhouses, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain

trees.story: This tree is 289 years old and it fits on a table. It was started in 1737, when Boston was still a colonial port, and it has spent every one of those years in a pot, watered and pruned by somebody, without a gap. Larz Anderson, a Harvard graduate and American ambassador to Japan, bought it from the Yokohama Nursery Company around 1913 with roughly 39 other bonsai and shipped the lot home to his estate in Brookline, where it stood on his terraces for 24 years. After he and his wife Isabel died, the collection passed to the Arnold Arboretum, which eventually built a pavilion to house it. A cutting taken in 2017 is displayed beside it, the same tree at nine years old and at 289. Two things to know before you go. The 1737 date comes from Anderson's own records rather than from any independent dating, so it is one careful line of evidence repeated by everyone since, not two. And the pavilion rotates around 30 trees through its display every two or three weeks from mid April to late October, so this particular one is not guaranteed to be out on the day you arrive; the pavilion posts what is currently on view. It is ten minutes on foot from Forest Hills, and the Arboretum around it is worth the trip whatever is in the display that week.
verified_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larz_Anderson_Bonsai_Collection (citing Larz Anderson's own records: 'the oldest of these Hinoki Cypress was started in 1737')

https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/04/23/boston-arnold-arboretum-bonsai-trees-spring (WBUR News, 2026-04-23, independent of the Arboretum, confirms the '289-year-old hinoki cypress' on display this season and quotes curator Chris Copeland calling it one of the oldest cultivated bonsai in North America, second only to three at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden)

https://jamaicaplainnews.com/2024/04/16/nearly-three-centuries-old-bonsai-cypress-lives-at-arnold-arboretum/666645 (Jamaica Plain News, 2024-04-16, local outlet independent of the Arboretum, corroborates the 1737 origin and confirms it alive and maintained by bonsai master Jun Imabayashi)

The bonsai itself is on view only mid-April through late October at the Bonsai and Penjing Pavilion, and staff rotate roughly 30 trees through the display every two to three weeks, so this specific specimen is not guaranteed to be out on any given visit; the pavilion posts what is currently on view.

trees.name: The Sapporo Katsuras

location.address: Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University, along Meadow Road
location.neighbourhood: Meadow Road, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain

trees.story: These two trees began as seed in a packet posted from Sapporo. William S. Clark, president of Massachusetts Agricultural College and the man who left his Japanese students the parting line "Boys, be ambitious", went to Hokkaido in 1876 to help found what is now Hokkaido University. He collected katsura seed there and sent a share to his friend Charles Sprague Sargent, the Arnold Arboretum's first director. It arrived in 1878, six years after the Arboretum itself existed at all, and the two multi stemmed trees on Meadow Road are what grew from it. They are the oldest katsuras in a collection of 35 and among the oldest documented anywhere in North America. Come in October. Katsura leaves turn apricot and gold, and as they fall and dry they give off a smell most people read as burnt sugar or candy floss; you often catch it before you find the tree. Winter is worth a different look, the silvery grey bark peeling away in narrow rectangular sheets and curved seed follicles hanging on into the cold before the wind takes the seed. Sargent went to Hokkaido himself in 1892 and wrote about katsura as a defining tree of the island's wet lowland woods. One note on sourcing: both accounts here are the Arboretum's own, a plant record and an Arnoldia article rather than two unconnected institutions, though the article's author visited and describes both trees alive and in health.

best_time.label: October, when the falling leaves turn apricot gold and smell of burnt sugar

verified_sources: https://arboretum.harvard.edu/plant-bios/katsura/ (accessions 882*A and 882*B, seed from Professor W. S. Clark, arrived 1878)
https://arboretum.harvard.edu/arnoldia-stories/katsura-in-winter (Arnoldia, confirms both trees living 'along Meadow Road', describes their winter bark and persistent seed follicles firsthand)
trees.access: Free, public arboretum, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Forest Hills MBTA station (Orange Line), roughly 15-20 minute walk via the Forest Hills Gate to Meadow Road, or the Arborway entrance

trees.name: The Longfellow Linden

location.address: Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters National Historic Site, 105 Brattle Street, Cambridge, MA
location.neighbourhood: Cambridge (within the day-trip boundary of Boston, roughly 20-25 minutes via Red Line to Harvard Square then a short walk)

trees.story: In the summer of 1844 Henry Wadsworth Longfellow came home to find that workmen had "lopped away the long low branches of my Linden tree, misunderstanding my directions", and he wrote it up in his journal as a small catastrophe. The tree outlived him. It went into the ground around 1800 to 1810, planted by Andrew Craigie, who owned the Brattle Street estate before the poet came to it in 1843, and it stands on the East Lawn of a house that had served as George Washington's headquarters during the siege of Boston a generation before the linden existed. Fanny Longfellow wrote in 1843 of wanting "a linden avenue in which my poet intends to pace in his old age". This is the only tree of that avenue still standing. By 1846 he was describing her reading Heine underneath it. The National Park Service puts it at 82 feet, against roughly 60 for the species, with a trunk 84 inches through, and rates its condition fair to poor: the trunk cavity is filled, cables carry the branches, heavy pruning comes round every five years. Since the early 2000s the park has been growing a genetically identical cutting against the day it goes. The grounds are free and open in daylight; only the house tours are ticketed.

best_time.label: late June into July, when the lime flowers and the whole East Lawn smells of it

trees.access: Free; National Historic Site grounds are open to the public daily during daylight hours (house tours are separately ticketed but the East Lawn where the tree stands is publicly accessible)
trees.transport: MBTA Red Line to Harvard Square, then about 8-10 minutes on foot down Brattle Street

trees.name: The Houghton Beech

location.address: 1000-1008 Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge, MA (between Harvard Square and Central Square, on the site of the former Houghton estate, now part of MIT/University Park land)
location.neighbourhood: Cambridge, Mid-Cambridge/University Park (within the day-trip boundary; on the Red Line corridor)

trees.story: This is Cambridge's only living Historic Landmark, and it was made one in 1985 to stop a building. A developer's plans for the site would have taken a third of the copper beech's crown and finished it off, so about thirty neighbours formed a group called the Friends of the Beech Tree and petitioned the city; the Historical Commission designated the tree itself, the legal instrument normally reserved for buildings. The Harvard Crimson, reporting from the October 1985 hearing, called it 203 years old, which puts its planting around 1782 and makes it roughly 240 now. That figure carries more weight than the biography printed around it in the same article, which has Henry O. Houghton serving as mayor decades before he founded the Riverside Press. A 2018 local survey of Cambridge trees offers a looser "planted 150+ years ago", a lower bound rather than a contradiction. Houghton planted three beeches on his family estate here. This is the one left. MIT bought the property in the 1970s and took down the buildings, and the tree stayed, which is how a private estate specimen ended up standing on a public sidewalk on Massachusetts Avenue between Central and Harvard. Most of Boston's notable trees sit inside curated collections. This one you walk past on the way to the bus.

best_time.label: May, when the new leaves open translucent red before they darken to purple-black

trees.access: Free; stands beside a public sidewalk on Massachusetts Avenue, fully visible and reachable at any time
trees.transport: MBTA Red Line to Central Square, then about 8 minutes on foot along Mass Ave toward Harvard Square
